title: Binary Tree Cameras
description: Brute force to optimized: trying every subset of camera placements versus a greedy bottom-up DFS with three coverage states.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given the root of a binary tree, install cameras on tree nodes such that every node in the tree is covered (a camera at a node covers itself, its parent, and its direct children). Return the minimum number of cameras needed.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","root of a binary tree"],["Output","The minimum number of cameras needed to cover every node"],["Key Insight","A greedy, bottom-up placement, adding a camera at a parent ONLY when forced (a child is not yet covered), is provably optimal"],["Constraints","Up to 1000 nodes"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Minimum number of cameras to cover a tree, each covering itself, parent, and children\"","A greedy bottom-up (post-order) DFS: decide whether to place a camera at a node based only on its children's already-determined states, deferring the decision as long as possible"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Placing cameras as deep (as close to the leaves) as possible, and only when strictly necessary, is optimal, since a camera placed lower in the tree can cover more potential nodes (its parent AND its own children) than being forced to place one prematurely. Each node needs to be tracked in one of three states: not yet covered by any camera, covered but has no camera itself, or has a camera itself.

blocks.title: Analogy: Placing Security Guards to Watch a Building's Floors, Covering Above and Below
blocks.text: Picture placing security guards on specific floors of a building, where each guard watches their own floor, the floor directly above, and the floor directly below. Working from the TOP floors DOWN to the ground floor, a guard should only be placed on a floor when strictly necessary (some floor below is not yet covered), since placing guards as low as possible covers the most floors per guard.

blocks.caption: Greedy bottom-up: place a camera at a parent only when forced by an uncovered child

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: tree = [0, 0, , 0, 0] (root with two children, one of which has two children of its own)
Minimum cameras = 1. A single camera at the middle level covers everything.
Example: tree = [0, 0, null, 0, null, 0, null, null, 0]
Minimum cameras = 2.
5. How Should We Think?

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A node can be in exactly one of three states: NOT_COVERED (no camera sees it yet), COVERED_NO_CAM (covered by a nearby camera, but has none itself), or HAS_CAM (has its own camera).

Observation 2: An empty (null) child should be treated as COVERED_NO_CAM, since it needs no monitoring and should never force a camera placement on its own.

Observation 3: If EITHER child of the current node is NOT_COVERED, a camera MUST be placed at the current node (there is no other way to cover that child), and this node becomes HAS_CAM.

Observation 4: Otherwise, if EITHER child HAS_CAM, the current node is automatically covered by that camera (COVERED_NO_CAM), no camera needed here.

Observation 5: Otherwise (both children are COVERED_NO_CAM, with no cameras nearby), the current node itself becomes NOT_COVERED, deferring the decision up to its own parent.

Observation 6: Finally, if the ROOT itself ends up NOT_COVERED after this entire bottom-up process, one additional camera must be placed at the root.
This leads to a post-order DFS assigning one of three states per node, greedily placing a camera only when a child is not yet covered, with a final check at the root.
6. Brute Force Solution
Conceptually, try every possible subset of nodes as camera placements, checking full coverage for each, and keep the smallest valid subset found.

codes.python:
# Conceptually: enumerate every possible subset of nodes as candidate
# camera placements (2^n subsets), checking whether each subset covers
# every node (itself, its parent, and its children), keeping the
# smallest valid subset found. Correct, but astronomically slow, since
# there are 2^n subsets to consider for n up to 1000 nodes.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Trying every subset directly implements the definition of "find the minimum covering set" literally.
This costs O(2 raised to n), utterly infeasible for up to 1000 nodes; a greedy bottom-up DFS finds the provably optimal answer in linear time instead.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(2 raised to n) to enumerate all subsets.
Space: O(n) per subset check.
Limitation: a greedy bottom-up DFS, deferring camera placement as long as possible, is provably optimal and runs in linear time.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Define dfs(node), returning one of three states. A null node returns COVERED_NO_CAM (needs no coverage). Otherwise, recursively compute the left and right children's states. If either is NOT_COVERED, increment the camera count and return HAS_CAM for this node. Otherwise, if either child HAS_CAM, return COVERED_NO_CAM (this node is covered by that camera). Otherwise, return NOT_COVERED (defer the decision upward). After the DFS completes at the root, if the root itself ended up NOT_COVERED, increment the camera count once more (a camera must be placed at the root itself).
Use a greedy post-order DFS with three node states, placing a camera only when a child is not yet covered, plus a final root check.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for [0,0,null,0,0] (root A, left child B, B has two leaf children C, D)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Node","Children states","Decision"],"rows":[["C, D (leaves, null children)","both children null, COVERED_NO_CAM","both return NOT_COVERED (no camera nearby)"],["B","C and D are NOT_COVERED","camera placed here, B returns HAS_CAM, count=1"],["A (root)","B is HAS_CAM, right child null is COVERED_NO_CAM","A returns COVERED_NO_CAM, no camera needed"],["Final check","root state is COVERED_NO_CAM, not NOT_COVERED","no extra camera needed, final answer 1"]]}

blocks.text: Why This Works

Deferring a camera placement as long as possible (only placing one when a child would otherwise go uncovered) is optimal because a camera placed lower in the tree always covers at least as much as one placed higher (it still covers its own parent, plus its own children, which a higher placement cannot reach); treating null children as automatically covered correctly prevents leaf nodes from being forced to have cameras placed directly on them unnecessarily, letting their PARENT take on that responsibility instead, which is always at least as good.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n).
Space: O(h) recursion depth.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Try every subset of nodes","O(2^n)","O(n) per subset","Correct, but utterly infeasible."],["Greedy bottom-up DFS with three states","O(n)","O(h) recursion depth","The expected, provably optimal solution."]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Binary Tree Cameras is a classic greedy-on-trees problem: deferring a decision (placing a camera) as long as possible, forcing it only when strictly necessary, is provably optimal here.
Common Mistakes

items: Treating a null child as NOT_COVERED instead of COVERED_NO_CAM, which would incorrectly force cameras onto every leaf node.
Forgetting the final check at the root: if the root itself ends up NOT_COVERED after the DFS, one more camera is still needed.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A single node tree","Needs exactly one camera (that single node ends up NOT_COVERED, forcing the final root check to add one)."],["A long chain (each node has exactly one child)","Cameras are placed roughly every third node, alternating states down the chain."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "defer placing a camera as long as possible, forcing it only when a child would otherwise be uncovered" demonstrates the key greedy insight and why it is optimal.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "minimum cameras to cover a tree, each covering itself, parent, and children", think: a greedy bottom-up DFS with three coverage states per node.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you formally prove that this greedy bottom-up strategy is optimal (an exchange argument)?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: House Robber III and other tree-DP problems that assign states per node based on children's states.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force subset search costs O(2^n), utterly infeasible; the greedy bottom-up DFS costs O(n), the standard, provably optimal solution.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: greedy bottom-up (post-order) DFS with a small fixed set of per-node states.
Core Idea: defer placing a camera as long as possible, forcing one only when a child would otherwise be left uncovered.
Time: O(2^n) for the brute force, O(n) for the greedy approach.
Space: O(n) per subset for the brute force, O(h) recursion depth for the greedy approach.
Most Important Observation: a lower camera placement always covers at least as much as a higher one, making deferral optimal.
One line memory trick: place a camera only when forced, as late as possible.
